title: Ziervogel v. Royal Packing Co.
lead: A collision defendant knows about claimed blood-pressure harm before trial, yet its repeated objections preserve the distinction between actual notice and specifically pleaded special damages.

actors.name: Royal Packing Co.
actors.role: Employer of the tractor-trailer driver and defendant.

actors.name: Dr. Leo A. Will
actors.role: Defense physician who examined the plaintiff and reported to the insurer’s agent.

proceedings: A jury awarded $2,000, and the trial court denied a new trial.
The Missouri appellate court reversed and remanded on December 20, 1949.
Rehearing or transfer was denied January 20, 1950; only the assigned edited rehearing passage is available.
limits: The complete reproduced original opinion was available, but the reporter facsimile and complete rehearing opinion were not. Fault was not retried on appeal, and reversal did not eliminate all recoverable injury claims.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An intersection collision leads to competing negligence pleadings
sections.cue: Which injuries appeared in the petition?
paragraphs: The plaintiff alleged an April 20, 1948 St. Louis collision at Vandeventer Avenue and North Market Street. She drove a Studebaker north; Royal Packing’s employee drove a tractor-trailer west. Her petition alleged failures of lookout, warning, speed, stopping, swerving, and right of way, and injuries to neck, back, spine, and nervous system, other injuries, and permanently impaired earning capacity.

Royal Packing admitted directions and collision but denied the rest, asserting contributory negligence in observation, speed, control, and failure to obey a school stop sign. These were opposing allegations, not appellate findings of every asserted act. Both sides offered witnesses and medical evidence, and the jury awarded the plaintiff $2,000. After denial of a new trial, Royal Packing appealed without contesting sufficiency to submit negligence. The appellate court therefore did not recount all collision proof.

sections.title: Blood-pressure and shoulder evidence draws repeated objections
sections.cue: Why could Royal Packing not fairly claim surprise?
paragraphs: In opening, plaintiff’s counsel said the accident increased blood pressure. Royal Packing objected, requested discharge of the jury, and later objected to evidence of that condition and a shoulder injury. Neither elevated pressure nor aggravation of an existing pressure condition was specifically pleaded. No alleged injury made the condition necessarily or inevitably follow, and the evidence did not establish inevitability. The unpleaded shoulder claim posed the same problem.

Before trial the plaintiff told the insurer’s claim agent about the pressure claim. Defense physician Dr. Leo A. Will examined her and reported to that agent, and the defendant deposed her. The appellate court expressly acknowledged absence of genuine surprise. But she neither amended the petition nor sought leave, though amendment might have been available on appropriate terms. Advance knowledge did not itself perform the missing pleading step.

sections.title: McCullen enforces a specific requirement within a liberal pleading code
sections.cue: Why did federal analogies and general justice provisions not change the result?
paragraphs: Judge McCullen applied Missouri’s historical § 52, Mo. R.S.A. § 847.52, requiring specific statement of special-damage items. An injury neither alleged nor necessarily resulting from an alleged injury was special damage requiring its own statement. The textbook’s bracketed Rule 55.19 reference modernized the citation; it was not the original provision.

The plaintiff invoked Code §§ 35 and 36’s concise, direct, short-and-plain allegations and § 57’s substantial-justice construction. General liberalization did not nullify the specific retained requirement. Earlier decisions remained relevant because the new code preserved their principle.

She also invoked federal illustrative Form 10 and Missouri’s borrowing from Federal Rules, arguing that discovery could supply detail. The court subordinated those analogies to explicit state text. It neither equated all state and federal procedure nor offered a comprehensive modern account of Rules 8 and 9(g).

sections.title: Responsive evidence does not waive an objection already overruled
paragraphs: Royal Packing introduced its own pressure evidence only after repeated objections failed. The court held that meeting an issue forced into trial was not voluntary invitation of error or abandonment of the preserved challenge. It also considered the Code’s bar on reversal for nonprejudicial error and found material prejudice here; it did not make every pleading defect automatically reversible.

The evidentiary ruling made a separate challenge to instruction 8 about pressure and shoulder injuries unnecessary. The court rejected a distinct objection that instructions 1 and 2 assumed which vehicle entered first: they conditioned propositions on the jury’s findings, and instruction 9 expressly reserved facts to the jury. Repeating qualifications at every clause would add clutter rather than clarity.

On December 20, 1949, the court reversed the $2,000 judgment and remanded for prejudicial admission of unpleaded special-damage evidence. Presiding Judge Anderson and Judge Hughes concurred without separate writing. It did not find Royal Packing nonnegligent or deny every injury.

sections.title: The available rehearing excerpt preserves the same pleading distinction
paragraphs: The assigned edited rehearing passage reports an argument that Missouri copied Federal Rule 9(g) and should adopt federal construction. McCullen answered that neither the plaintiff nor the court found an in-point decision and that the plain language did not allow pleading only general damages while recovering special damages. The textbook brackets denial, and the reproduced header dates denial of rehearing or transfer January 20, 1950.

The complete rehearing writing and original reporter images are unavailable here; the excerpt cannot certify every later argument or qualification. The five attached editorial notes distinguish special damages from fraud particularity, compare general and consequential losses, pose hypotheticals, discuss special damage as a substantive element, and address attorney-fee motions under Rule 54. Those are teaching materials, not additional holdings or independently audited cited cases.
